title: Signature Eclipse Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Eclipse bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its case is 36 centimetres tall in dark walnut, with a brass handle and a dial whose chapter ring is split into a light half and a dark half to mark day and night.

Mechanism: A spring barrel drives an anchor escapement with a 26 centimetre pendulum, and a day-night disc behind the dial aperture turns once per 24 hours. The eclipse hand points to the light or dark half of the dial to show whether the hour falls in day or night.

Maintenance: Wind the clock weekly, keep it level on its bracket, and dust the case with a soft cloth. The day-night disc is set by hand from local sunrise and sunset times and needs no other attention.

Build and restoration: The design is built for service: the dial lifts off on two screws and the movement slides out on rails. Tools: screwdrivers, hand puller, oil, tweezers, and a spirit level.

title: Signature Twin-Bell Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Twin-Bell bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. It strikes the hour alternately on two bells of different pitch, so the ear can follow the count even in a noisy room, in a case 34 centimetres tall.

Mechanism: Two strike hammers, one for each bell, are lifted alternately by the strike train, giving a high-low pattern through the hour count. The going train is a standard spring-barrel anchor movement with a short pendulum.

Maintenance: Keep both bells free of dust and check that each hammer falls cleanly on its bell. If one bell sounds dull, the hammer gap for that bell needs adjustment, not the bell itself.

Build and restoration: The bells are mounted on a removable bar so either can be replaced without stripping the movement. Tools: screwdrivers, hammer-setting gauge, oil, and a pitch reference.

title: Signature Meridian Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Meridian bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its dial carries a second, smaller chapter ring showing the time at a chosen reference meridian, set by hand when the clock is installed.

Mechanism: The reference hand is driven from the motion work through a 12-to-1 reduction so it turns once per twelve hours, and a setting knob on the dial back moves it independently of the main hands. The going train is spring-driven with an anchor escapement.

Maintenance: Set the reference hand once and leave it; it needs no daily attention. Wind weekly and keep the clock level, as with any bracket clock.

Build and restoration: The setting knob is reached through the dial back without removing the movement. Tools: screwdrivers, setting key, oil, and a reference time source.

title: Signature Harbour Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Harbour bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its dial adds a tide ring marked high and low water, driven to follow the roughly 12 hour 25 minute tidal cycle, in a salt-air-resistant oiled oak case.

Mechanism: The tide hand is driven from the motion work through a reduction train approximating the tidal period, and it is corrected by hand against published tide times once a week. The main timekeeping is a spring-barrel anchor movement.

Maintenance: Wipe the case with an oiled cloth in damp rooms and check the tide hand weekly against local tide times. Keep the clock out of direct sea spray, which corrodes brass dials.

Build and restoration: The tide ring is a separate dial layer that lifts off for cleaning. Tools: oiled cloth, screwdrivers, oil, and a tide table.

title: Signature Botanical Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Botanical bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its case is carved with leaves and seed heads in limewood, finished in clear wax, and its dial corners carry cast leaf spandrels instead of the usual scrollwork.

Mechanism: The movement is a spring-driven anchor movement with a short pendulum and an hour strike on a single bell. The carving is decorative only and does not touch the movement, so the clock services like any standard bracket clock.

Maintenance: Dust carved work with a soft brush, never with a damp cloth, and wax the case once a year. Keep the clock out of strong sunlight, which fades limewood unevenly.

Build and restoration: Carving repairs use matching limewood and hide glue, with the grain followed across the repair. Tools: soft brushes, carving chisels, hide glue, wax, and fine abrasive paper.

title: Signature Chime-Select Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Chime-Select bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. A dial-side lever lets the owner choose Westminster quarters, a simple hour-only strike, or silence, without opening the case.

Mechanism: The lever moves a detent that either engages the chime barrel, engages only the hour strike, or blocks both releases. The going train runs in all three modes, so the timekeeping never stops when the sound is changed.

Maintenance: Change the chime mode only when the clock is not in warning, in the minutes before a quarter, to avoid jamming the detent. If a mode fails to engage, the detent spring needs adjustment.

Build and restoration: The selector is reached through the case side door and adjusts with a single screw. Tools: screwdrivers, bending pliers, oil, and a chime test chart.

title: Signature Repeat-and-Chime Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Repeat-and-Chime bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Pulling its cord repeats the last quarter chime as well as the hour, so the full time can be heard in the dark.

Mechanism: The repeat cord winds a small spring that re-runs the chime barrel under rack control, then the hour strike follows. The repeat train is separate from the normal chime train, so repeating never disturbs the next quarter.

Maintenance: Pull the cord smoothly and let it return on its own; do not pull twice in quick succession. Keep the cord dry and replace it at the first sign of fraying.

Build and restoration: The repeat spring and cord path are laid out on a single plate for easy tracing. Tools: cord, tweezers, screwdrivers, oil, and a repeat test chart.

title: Signature Glass-Panel Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Glass-Panel bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its side panels are glazed so the going, strike and chime trains can be watched at work, and the back door is glazed as well.

Mechanism: The movement is a standard three-train spring-barrel movement with an anchor escapement, mounted on an open frame so every wheel is visible. The glass does not affect the timekeeping, but it makes beat faults and strike faults visible as well as audible.

Maintenance: Clean the glass with a dry microfibre cloth and keep fingers off the movement, since skin oils mark brass. Service intervals are the same as for a closed-case bracket clock.

Build and restoration: The glazed panels lift out on brass clips for cleaning without tools. Tools: microfibre cloth, screwdrivers, oil, and tweezers.

title: Signature Travelling Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Travelling bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. It has a locking pendulum clamp, a screwed-down movement, and a padded carrying case, so it can travel without the pendulum swinging free.

Mechanism: The pendulum clamps against a felt pad when the case lever is turned, and the movement is held by two thumb screws instead of friction alone. The going train is a spring-barrel anchor movement with a 22 centimetre pendulum for a compact case.

Maintenance: Always clamp the pendulum before moving the clock, and unclamp it only after the clock is level on its bracket. Wind the clock after travel, since a journey can let the spring down unevenly.

Build and restoration: The clamp is adjusted by a single screw that sets the felt pressure. Tools: screwdrivers, felt pads, oil, and a spirit level.

title: Signature Observatory Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Observatory bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its dial is regulator-style, with a large minute ring and small separate hour and seconds rings, for reading the time to the minute at a glance.

Mechanism: The minute hand is driven directly from the centre wheel, while the hour and seconds hands are driven through reduction wheels from the same motion work. The escapement is an anchor with a 28 centimetre pendulum for a steadier beat.

Maintenance: Read the minute ring first and the small rings second, and set the clock from the minute hand. Wind weekly and keep the clock level, since a regulator dial shows rate errors plainly.

Build and restoration: The dial layers separate for cleaning, with the minute ring outermost. Tools: screwdrivers, hand puller, oil, and a timing reference.

title: Signature Annual Calendar Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Annual Calendar bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its calendar shows day, date and month, and needs correction only once a year, at the end of February.

Mechanism: The calendar mechanism uses a 31-tooth date wheel plus month and day wheels stepped by fingers from the motion work, with a February cam that shortens the month. The going train is a spring-barrel anchor movement.

Maintenance: Correct the calendar on the first of March if February has run short, and never correct it between 9 at night and 3 in the morning when the fingers are engaged. Wind weekly as usual.

Build and restoration: The calendar wheels are reached from the dial back and step by hand for testing. Tools: tweezers, oil, screwdrivers, and a calendar chart.

title: Signature Moonphase Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Moonphase bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its moon disc is painted with a star field and two moons, and a shaped aperture shows the moon's phase against a deep blue ground.

Mechanism: The disc is driven by a 59-tooth wheel from the motion work, advancing one tooth per day for a 29.5 day cycle. The going train is a spring-barrel anchor movement with an hour strike on a bell.

Maintenance: Set the disc from a known new moon and correct it by one day every two to three years. Keep the painted disc dry and out of sunlight.

Build and restoration: The disc lifts off its arbor for repainting without stripping the movement. Tools: fine brushes, moonphase paint, tweezers, and a lunar calendar.

title: Signature Silent-Night Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Silent-Night bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Its night-silence cam is adjustable by the owner, so the silent hours can be set to match the household instead of a fixed 10 to 8 pattern.

Mechanism: A cam on the hour wheel carries two adjustable pins that define the silent window, and a detent blocks the strike release while the cam is between the pins. The going train runs on silently through the window.

Maintenance: Set the pins with the clock stopped and the hands at noon, then test through a full day by hand before relying on the silence. Do not move the pins while the strike is in warning.

Build and restoration: The cam pins are set with a small key supplied with the clock. Tools: setting key, screwdrivers, oil, and a 24-hour test chart.

title: Signature Concert Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Concert bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. On the hour it plays a short tune on a pinned cylinder and comb, in addition to striking the hour on a bell.

Mechanism: The musical train is a fourth train beside the going, strike and chime trains, with a pinned brass cylinder that lifts the teeth of a steel comb as it turns. The tune plays once per hour and can be silenced by a lever.

Maintenance: Keep the comb free of dust and never touch the pinned cylinder with bare fingers, since the pins bend easily. If a note fails, the comb tooth is usually dusty or misaligned, not broken.

Build and restoration: Comb teeth are tuned by filing the underside of the tooth, a little at a time, against a pitch reference. Tools: tuning file, tweezers, oil, magnification, and a pitch reference.

title: Signature Restoration-Ready Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Restoration-Ready bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. Every part is made in a standard size, the movement is held by four screws, and a service manual is fixed inside the case door.

Mechanism: The movement is a spring-barrel anchor movement with a short pendulum, hour strike, and quarter chime, laid out on two plates with all pivots reachable from the back. No part needs a special tool beyond standard clockmaker's tools.

Maintenance: Follow the manual's service interval of five years, and record each service on the card inside the door. Replacement parts are standard sizes, so a worn wheel or pinion can be swapped without remaking the train.

Build and restoration: The manual lists every wheel's tooth count and every pivot's size for ordering parts. Tools: screwdrivers, tweezers, oil, bushing tools, and the case manual.

title: Signature Grand Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications: The Signature Grand bracket clock is an original Signature design, not an authentic historical clock. It is the largest Signature bracket design at 44 centimetres tall, with grande sonnerie striking, quarter chiming, and a visible pendulum behind a glazed lower door.

Mechanism: Three trains run the going, the grande sonnerie strike, and the quarter chime, with a mode selector offering grande sonnerie, petite sonnerie, and silent. The anchor escapement uses a 30 centimetre pendulum for the steadiest beat in the Signature bracket range.

Maintenance: Wind all three trains fully each week, since the strike and chime trains do heavy work. Keep the clock level and the glazed door closed, to keep dust off the visible pendulum.

Build and restoration: The three trains are laid out side by side for servicing in order. Tools: screwdrivers, tweezers, oil, beat amplifier, and a strike test chart.
